neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.title: Neutron Electric Dipole Moment Upper Bound
neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.description: This value represents the current experimental upper limit for the magnitude of the neutron's electric dipole moment.
neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.conceptual_definition: The electric dipole moment (EDM) of a fundamental particle like the neutron is a measure of the separation of positive and negative charges within it. A non-zero EDM would imply a violation of both parity (P) and time-reversal ($T$) symmetries, and by the CPT theorem, also CP symmetry. This value is an experimental upper bound, meaning no EDM has been definitively detected for the neutron at this sensitivity.
neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.interpretation: The extremely small upper bound on the neutron EDM, $1.8 \times 10^{-26} \text{ e}\cdot\text{cm}$, places stringent constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. Many proposed extensions, such as supersymmetry, predict EDMs significantly larger than this bound. The continued absence of a detected neutron EDM at this level suggests that new sources of CP violation, if they exist, must be very weak or occur at energy scales much higher than currently probed.
neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.limits_and_boundary: This value itself is an experimental upper limit. It defines the current boundary of experimental sensitivity for the neutron's electric dipole moment. Future experiments aim to push this bound even lower, seeking to detect a non-zero EDM or further constrain new physics.
neutron-electric-dipole-moment-upper-bou.symmetry_origin: A non-zero electric dipole moment would signify a violation of both parity (P) and time-reversal ($T$) symmetries. By the CPT theorem, this also implies a violation of charge-parity (CP) symmetry. The Standard Model predicts a neutron EDM far below current experimental sensitivity, making this bound a crucial test for new physics that introduces additional sources of CP violation.

semantic_variables.neutron_edm_bound_value: The numerical value of the current experimental upper bound for the neutron's electric dipole moment. This value is typically expressed in units of electron charge times centimeter (e\cdot cm), which are non-SI units commonly used in particle physics for EDMs.

virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.title: Virtual Work of an Actual Force
virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.description: This term represents the infinitesimal work done by an actual force acting on a particle during a virtual displacement. It is a scalar product of the force and the virtual displacement.
virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.conceptual_definition: In the context of virtual work, this term quantifies the work that would be done by a real, physical force acting on a specific particle if that particle were to undergo an infinitesimal, imaginary displacement consistent with the system's constraints. It is a scalar quantity, representing the projection of the force vector onto the virtual displacement vector.
virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.interpretation: This specific term, $\mathbf{F}_i^{(actual)} \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i$, is the contribution of the actual force $\mathbf{F}_i^{(actual)}$ acting on the $i$-th particle to the total virtual work of the system. When summed over all particles and set to zero, it forms the basis of the Principle of Virtual Work for equilibrium. It signifies the work done by a real force over a hypothetical, instantaneous displacement that does not necessarily occur in time but is kinematically possible.
virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.limits_and_boundary: This term is typically considered for infinitesimal virtual displacements ($\delta \mathbf{r}_i \to 0$). It applies to systems in static equilibrium or, more generally, to systems where the virtual displacements are consistent with the system's constraints. It does not involve time, as virtual displacements are instantaneous and not necessarily real motions.
virtual-work-of-an-actual-force-a4b72fa7.symmetry_origin: The Principle of Virtual Work, of which this term is a component, is a variational principle deeply connected to the concept of equilibrium and the balance of forces. It can be seen as a statement of energy conservation for virtual displacements, where no actual work is done by the net force during a virtual displacement at equilibrium.

semantic_variables.F_i^(actual): The actual, physical force vector acting on the $i$-th particle of the system, measured in Newtons (N). This force can include applied forces, constraint forces, and any other real forces.

condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.title: Condition for Static Equilibrium
condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.description: This equation states that the vector sum of all actual forces acting on a particle or system is zero, representing a state of equilibrium.
condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.conceptual_definition: In physics, this equation defines the state of static equilibrium for a particle or a rigid body. It implies that the object is either at rest or moving with constant velocity, though in the context of virtual work, it specifically refers to static equilibrium. For a system of particles, it means the net force on each individual particle is zero.
condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.interpretation: Physically, \mathbf{F}^{(actual)} = 0 signifies that there is no net external force acting on the object or system. Consequently, according to Newton's first law of motion, the object's acceleration is zero. If the object was initially at rest, it will remain at rest; if it was in motion, it would continue in motion with constant velocity. In the context of the Principle of Virtual Work, this condition is specifically applied to systems in static equilibrium, where all components are stationary.
condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.limits_and_boundary: This equation applies to systems in inertial frames of reference. It is valid for both point particles and rigid bodies. For deformable bodies, it applies to each infinitesimal volume element. It is a fundamental condition for equilibrium in classical mechanics.
condition-for-static-equilibrium-9644667.symmetry_origin: This equation is a direct consequence of Newton's First Law of Motion. It is related to the conservation of linear momentum: if the net force is zero, the linear momentum of the system is conserved. Translational symmetry in space implies conservation of linear momentum.

semantic_variables.F_actual: The vector sum of all actual forces acting on a particle or system, measured in Newtons (N).

lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.title: Lorentz Factor and Non-Relativistic Limit
lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.description: Defines the Lorentz factor, a key quantity in special relativity, and shows its approximation for low velocities.
lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.conceptual_definition: The Lorentz factor, denoted by $\gamma$, is a dimensionless quantity that quantifies the magnitude of relativistic effects such as time dilation, length contraction, and relativistic mass increase. It depends solely on the relative velocity between two inertial frames of reference and the speed of light in vacuum. It serves as a scaling factor for spacetime intervals and energy-momentum in special relativity.
lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.interpretation: This equation defines the Lorentz factor, $\gamma$, which is always greater than or equal to 1. When the relative velocity $v$ is zero, $\gamma = 1$, indicating no relativistic effects. As $v$ increases and approaches the speed of light $c$, $\gamma$ approaches infinity, signifying that relativistic effects become increasingly pronounced. The approximation $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2} is valid for velocities much smaller than $c$, showing that for everyday speeds, $\gamma$ is very close to 1, and relativistic effects are negligible, thus recovering classical mechanics.
lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.limits_and_boundary: The velocity $v$ must be less than the speed of light $c$ for the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ to be a real number. As $v$ approaches $c$, $\gamma$ tends towards infinity, implying that an object with mass cannot reach the speed of light. In the non-relativistic limit, where $v \ll c$, the Lorentz factor approximates to $1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2}, which further simplifies to $1$ as $v$ becomes negligibly small compared to $c$.
lorentz-factor-and-non-relativistic-limi.symmetry_origin: The Lorentz factor arises directly from the fundamental postulates of special relativity: the principle of relativity and the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames. It is a consequence of the underlying Lorentz symmetry of spacetime, which dictates that the laws of physics are invariant under Lorentz transformations (rotations and boosts). This symmetry ensures the invariance of the spacetime interval, leading to the specific form of $\gamma$.

semantic_variables.v: Relative velocity between inertial frames (meters per second, m/s)
semantic_variables.c: Speed of light in vacuum (meters per second, m/s)

partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.title: Partial Derivative Operator
partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.description: The partial derivative operator with respect to the k-th coordinate, used to measure the rate of change of a multivariable function along a single dimension.
partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.conceptual_definition: In physics, the partial derivative operator $\partial_k$ signifies the rate of change of a function with respect to its k-th independent variable, while all other independent variables are held constant. It is a fundamental concept in calculus and is extensively used in field theories, fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and general relativity to describe how physical quantities vary in space and time. This operator allows for the analysis of complex systems by isolating the effect of individual parameters.
partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.interpretation: This operator is crucial for analyzing systems where physical quantities depend on multiple independent parameters, such as spatial coordinates or time. For instance, $\partial_x \Phi$ describes how a scalar field $\Phi$ changes as one moves along the x-axis, ignoring changes in y and z. It forms the basis for constructing more complex differential operators like the gradient, divergence, and curl, which are essential for formulating fundamental laws of physics in differential form. Its application is key to understanding local variations and gradients in physical fields.
partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.limits_and_boundary: The application of the partial derivative operator requires the function to be differentiable with respect to the chosen variable at the point of interest. For higher-order derivatives, the function must possess continuous partial derivatives up to that order (e.g., for Schwarz's theorem on mixed partials). It is typically applied to functions defined over continuous domains and is well-defined for smooth functions.
partial-derivative-operator-1650ef9c.symmetry_origin: While the partial derivative operator itself doesn't directly represent a symmetry, its application is fundamental to expressing physical laws that exhibit symmetries. For example, in coordinate transformations, the chain rule involving partial derivatives ensures that physical laws retain their form (covariance). The existence of continuous partial derivatives is a prerequisite for many conservation laws derived from variational principles via Noether's theorem, which links symmetries to conserved quantities.

semantic_variables.k: An integer index representing the specific independent variable or coordinate with respect to which the partial derivative is taken (dimensionless).

electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.title: Electric Potential of a Point Charge
electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.description: This equation describes the electric potential generated by a single point charge in a vacuum at a given distance from the charge.
electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.conceptual_definition: The electric potential, \Phi, at a point in space due to a point charge, q, is defined as the amount of work required per unit charge to move a test charge from infinity to that point. It is a scalar field that characterizes the electric field and is a measure of the potential energy per unit charge at a given location.
electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.interpretation: The formula $\Phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ indicates that the electric potential created by a point charge is directly proportional to the magnitude of the charge, q, and inversely proportional to the distance, r, from the charge. The constant $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ is Coulomb's constant, which depends on the permittivity of free space, \varepsilon_0. This inverse dependence on distance means the potential decreases as one moves further away from the charge, approaching zero at infinite distance.
electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid for a point charge in a vacuum or a linear, isotropic, homogeneous dielectric medium (by replacing \varepsilon_0 with \varepsilon). It is not applicable at the location of the point charge itself (r=0), where the potential theoretically diverges. As r approaches infinity, the potential \Phi(\mathbf{r}) approaches zero, which is the standard reference point for electric potential.
electric-potential-of-a-point-charge-3b4.symmetry_origin: The spherical symmetry of the electric potential around a point charge is a direct consequence of the spherical symmetry of the charge distribution itself. The potential depends only on the radial distance from the charge, not on angular position.

semantic_variables.\\Phi(\\mathbf{r}): Electric potential at position \mathbf{r}, measured in Volts (V). It represents the potential energy per unit charge at that point.
semantic_variables.q: Magnitude of the point charge, measured in Coulombs (C). This is the source of the electric potential.
semantic_variables.\\varepsilon_0: Permittivity of free space, a fundamental physical constant approximately equal to 8.854 \times 10^{-12} F/m (Farads per meter). It quantifies the ability of a vacuum to permit electric field lines.
semantic_variables.r: Scalar distance from the point charge to the observation point \mathbf{r}, measured in meters (m). It is the magnitude of the position vector \mathbf{r} from the charge.

change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.title: Change in Antiderivative Value
change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.description: This expression represents the net change in the value of a function G between two specific points in its domain, typically an initial and a final state.
change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.conceptual_definition: In physics, this term quantifies the total accumulation or depletion of a physical quantity G over a defined interval, where G is the antiderivative of some rate of change. It is the direct result of evaluating the antiderivative at the upper and lower limits of an integral, as prescribed by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.interpretation: This difference signifies the total effect or net change of a process occurring between an initial state (q_1, t_1) and a final state (q_2, t_2). For instance, if G represents energy, this is the change in energy. If G represents momentum, this is the change in momentum. It provides a direct measure of the total alteration in the quantity G, irrespective of the path taken between the two points, provided G is a state function.
change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.limits_and_boundary: This expression is valid when the function G is continuous and differentiable over the interval defined by (q_1, t_1) and (q_2, t_2). The points (q_1, t_1) and (q_2, t_2) serve as the boundary conditions for the evaluation of the antiderivative.
change-in-antiderivative-value-19c64a26.symmetry_origin: While this expression itself is a mathematical result, its application in physics often relates to conservation laws. For example, if dG/dt represents a force or a rate of work, then G(q_2, t_2) - G(q_1, t_1) might represent the change in potential energy or total work done, which are often linked to conservation principles (e.g., conservation of mechanical energy).

semantic_variables.G: The antiderivative function of a rate of change, representing a physical quantity whose total change is being calculated (units vary depending on the specific physical quantity).
semantic_variables.q_1: Initial generalized coordinate or spatial position (units vary, e.g., meters).
semantic_variables.q_2: Final generalized coordinate or spatial position (units vary, e.g., meters).
